core: History of Western philosophy, close reading of philosophical texts and critical argument
Metaphysics, epistemology, logic, philosophy of cognition and questions of free will
Ethics, philosophical anthropology and social and political philosophy
Philosophical research, independent essay, text analysis and dialogue

trace: Directly teaches propositional and predicate logic, quantifiers, truth tables and proof, supplying substantive formal reasoning for philosophical argument. Its further discrete mathematics and game modelling are complementary; it does not supply a complete philosophical-logic sequence.

Makes a specific complementary contribution to public ethics through institutions, power, participation, justice and competing sustainability responses. Governance-framework analysis and policy evaluation test how normative choices enter food, water and energy decisions; this is not a specialist environmental-philosophy seminar.

Makes a specific legal and normative complement through justice, legal positivism, rights, race and gender in law and the relation between law and social control. It connects questions of legitimate authority to actual legal argument without being counted as a dedicated philosophy course.

Provides a specific historical complement to political philosophy: modernity, nationalism, liberal and socialist ideologies, imperialism and decolonization, examined through historical contextualization and source analysis rather than as a substitute for the history of philosophy.

Directly examines philosophical justifications and critiques of human rights through natural law, natural rights, positivism, universality and dignity. Legal systems and cases test these claims. This mixed legal/philosophical course adds meaningful normative inquiry beyond the six dedicated philosophy courses.

Provides a specific institutional complement to political philosophy through constitutional authority, federalism, judicial review, fundamental rights and procedural fairness. Comparative constitutional analysis gives concrete institutional forms to the rights/authority questions; it is not counted as philosophical theory.

Provides a specific legal complement to political legitimacy beyond the state through EU competences, subsidiarity, proportionality, citizenship and remedies. Legal-source and case analysis tests how public authority is limited and rights implemented; this does not replace philosophical argument about legitimacy.

Directly studies historical and contemporary philosophical arguments about knowledge, ethics, mind, freedom, identity, time and meaning through close reading, conceptual analysis and argumentative essays. This substantive foundation is narrower than Radboud’s three-course historical sequence.

Directly studies moral and metaethical theories through close philosophical reading, comparison and independent argument. Kantian, consequentialist, virtue, feminist and contractarian ethics support questions about value, responsibility and practical judgment.

Directly studies minds, selves and conscious experience through historical and contemporary theories, including identity, physicalism, functionalism, perception and machine consciousness. Conceptual analysis and literature-based philosophical essays connect the empirical cognition strand to explicit philosophical argument.

Directly studies philosophical theories of emotion and their epistemic, moral, social and political significance. Historical and contemporary texts, phenomenological description and independent argument connect feeling, reason, moral judgment and human experience.

Directly studies free will, agency, determinism, responsibility, time and selfhood through close philosophical sources and independent argument. Scientific challenges and temporal asymmetries are considered within a philosophical investigation rather than counted as a full philosophy-of-science sequence.

Directly studies political philosophy through original texts, historical contextualization, comparison of arguments and the construction of a coherent normative position. Human nature, rights, authority, freedom and justice substantiate the public-life strand.

Makes a specific complementary contribution through competing realist, liberal, Marxist, constructivist and critical accounts of international power, colonial relationships and climate politics. Their assumptions and diplomatic simulation provide material for political-philosophical questions about justice beyond the state.

Makes a specific empirical complement to political philosophy through EU representation, legitimacy, democracy and interest influence. Legislative-document research and amendment analysis test how ideals of representation meet actual institutions; they are not normative philosophy themselves.

Makes a specific interdisciplinary complement to public ethics through structural violence, humanitarian law, human rights, reconciliation and transitional justice. Concept comparison, positionality and policy-option analysis develop reasoned engagement with conflict and peace.

Provides a specific social-theoretical complement through Marx, Weber, Durkheim and Du Bois, modernity, solidarity, identity and inequality. Theory-guided questions about social structures and exclusions complement normative accounts of society and human life.

Provides a specific methodological complement through qualitative knowledge, interpretation, ethics, positionality and reflexivity. Its empirical research design, coding and evidence limitations let students examine how claims about social meaning are established; it does not replace philosophical research or epistemology.

Provides a specific complement to ethical and political inquiry through environmental justice, feminist and anti-colonial perspectives, degrowth and peacebuilding, investigated with social-movement theories and concrete cases. No unprovided methods or philosophical-seminar depth is inferred.

Engages critical, neo-functionalist and decolonial social theories of civil society, hegemony, solidarity, public spheres and civil repair. Comparative theoretical and empirical analysis materially supports political-philosophical questions about public life without replacing normative philosophy.

Provides a specific empirical and ethical complement to philosophy of mind through comparative nervous systems, sentience, animal welfare, research ethics, sleep and mood. Biological explanation and the ethical appraisal of animal research support questions about minds and responsible inquiry.

Provides an empirical complement to philosophical questions about sensory experience through neural mechanisms of perception and goal-directed action. Its neuroscience and neuropsychology are considered fully without inventing more detailed activities than the course description supplies.

Provides an empirical complement to philosophical questions about attention, memory, emotion, control, social cognition and consciousness. Experimental design, critical literature and research ethics make a specific contribution to examining evidence about mind, without becoming a specialist philosophical-method course.

Provides a specific empirical complement to language and thought through speech production/comprehension, semantics, acquisition, impairments and experimental language research. The full description supports these topics and methods; the course is not relabelled as conceptual philosophy of language.

Provides a foundational empirical complement through neural mechanisms, psychological theories, self-concepts, mental disorders and research appraisal. This prepares the cognition strand and gives specific evidence with which philosophy of mind engages.

Studies classical rhetoric, argumentation, fallacies, text analysis and constructed public arguments through debate, writing and speech. This directly supports the analysis and communication of argument while retaining its rhetorical rather than philosophical-text focus.

Provides a specific interpretive complement through linguistic choices, modality, ideology, speech/thought presentation and text-world frameworks. Evidence-based stylistic analysis sharpens how arguments and perspectives are expressed, principally in literary texts; it is not specialist philosophical exegesis.

Provides a specific public-practice complement through persuasion ethics, framing, argumentation and reflective research on sustainability communication. Community-engaged projects test how argued positions reach and affect public audiences.

Provides a specific interpretive complement by examining literary value, constructed texts, point of view and formal meaning through close reading and critical-source integration. This supports reflective interpretation without being counted as philosophical-text instruction.

Provides a specific humanistic complement through literary treatments of mortality, freedom, identity, gender, community and civilization, including philosophical tales and satire. Comparative close reading connects human experience to the philosophical core; literary texts remain distinct from a canonical philosophy sequence.

Provides a specific interpretive-method complement by comparing humanist, feminist, Marxist, minority and psychoanalytic readings and applying a perspective in a text-based research project. Full consideration is given to its description without inventing further methods or assessments.

Provides a specific complement to questions of selfhood through memory, identity, embodiment, agency and autobiographical truth. Theory-guided close reading and life-narrative research examine how human experience is represented, without being counted as a philosophical-anthropology course.

alternatives.label: Philosophy, mind and human experience
alternatives.concept: A philosophical curriculum combining ethics, metaphysics, free will, political thought and close reading with empirical study of perception, cognition and language. Literary interpretation and life writing examine memory, identity and embodied experience alongside philosophical questions about the self. These complementary studies do not replace Radboud’s specialist philosophy seminars or required philosophical thesis.
alternatives.labelReason: The actual curriculum includes five philosophy courses, political philosophy, logic, cognitive science and interpretation; its label names the substantial philosophical and mind-related combination. Six direct philosophical courses carry45EC; empirical, literary, legal and social courses are separately identified complements, not substitutes for missing philosophical disciplines.
progression: Brain & Behavior in autumn2026 precedes Psycholinguistics in its sole planned spring2027 offering, and later Perception & Action and Higher Order Functions. Modern History in the first programme is replaced by spring2029Life & Travel Writing, specifically supporting identity, memory and embodiment and resolving the13autumn-course bottleneck. Sociology remainsautumn2026,Neurobiologyspring2027. Introductory philosophy,rhetoric andliterary interpretation precedetheiradvancedcourses. All formal prerequisites and actual six-term offerings pass.

alternatives.label: Ethics, political philosophy and public life
alternatives.concept: An ethics and political philosophy curriculum that tests ideas about justice, authority, rights and responsibility against constitutional and EU institutions, environmental justice and conflict. It exchanges the first curriculum’s sustained cognitive-science and literary interpretation strands for public and social questions supported by Radboud’s social/political philosophy, humanities-in-practice and Planet and Politics components. Philosophy of mind and emotion remain as questions about moral agency.
alternatives.labelReason: The course set links five philosophy courses and political philosophy to rights, institutions, social theory and environmental justice; the label describes this visible balance. Six direct philosophical courses carry45EC; empirical, literary, legal and social courses are separately identified complements, not substitutes for missing philosophical disciplines.
alternatives.distinctness: Nine substantively motivated replacements67.5EC replace the cognition and literary/life-interpretation strands with modern political history, constitutional/EU institutions, international politics, sustainability governance and environmental justice. The public-life programme changes academic priorities while retaining the philosophical core.
progression: Introductory philosophy, law and political thought provide a foundation for advanced ethics, social theory, EU politics and governance; Law, Society & Justice precedes formal law prerequisites, and all planned offerings are met.

candidates.label: Ethics, political philosophy and public life
candidates.reason: Current required Social and Political Philosophy, Planet and Politics and Humanities in Practice independently support this public-life concept; changing historical environmental examples and philosophy of psychiatry are not its generating basis.

candidates.label: Philosophical history, texts and independent argument
candidates.reason: Both completed programmes already teach close reading, the history of ideas, philosophical reasoning and public argument. UCR lacks an additional sustained specialist philosophical-text and philosophy-of-science sequence that would make a third 24-course curriculum academically distinct.

candidates.label: Logic and philosophy of science
candidates.reason: Discrete mathematics contains logic, and empirical methods examine evidence, but neither provides a sustained specialist philosophical-logic/epistemology/philosophy-of-science sequence. No third programme is defensible on that basis.

routeSelection.basis: Regular Dutch Filosofie current curriculum under the2026–2027 OER; not English PPS, shortened route or legacy4EC transition programme. The displayed three-of-four great-text and five-of-eight seminar choices are one coherent permitted selection.

selection.assessment: The broad first programme treats foundational philosophy through questions of mind, knowledge and human experience. The second changes nine courses and reorganises the evidence around ethics, politics, rights and public life. A third based on philosophical texts or reasoning is already integrated into both and would require unrelated substitutions for a distinct 24-course programme. Interest2160 (philosophy of science) is an explicit coverage gap, not an owned construction generator. The two retained responses have45EC direct philosophy each and differ by9courses/67.5EC; no third alternative is warranted. Fresh current-workbook challenge retained both concepts and the substantive course assessment, while repairing one selection in the first programme and the two organising concepts: each has six dedicated philosophical courses45EC, plus mixed philosophical human-rights study and specifically evidenced complements. All151activecourses considered for stronger philosophical implementation. Clinical psychology/psychopathology add empirical or clinical study rather than a missing specialist philosophy-of-psychiatry sequence; adding them would not establish a third independent concept. Historic seminar examples are not promoted to stable specialisations. Nine distinct courses67.5EC in each programme remain conceptually motivated. Psycholinguistics rescheduled rather than removed; no offering inferred. Life & Travel Writing adds specific memory/identity/embodiment/narrative analysis. Sole-offering Psycholinguistics can only follow autumn2026Brain & Behavior; retaining12autumn-onlycourses would then require13autumnslots. Replacing Modern History only in firstprogramme with this actual springcourse repairs the conflict without forcing an unrelated selection. Modern History retained inpublic-lifeprogramme forits evidencedpolitical-ideologyfunction.

notes.text: Radboud provides a structured sequence in philosophy, specialist seminars and a required philosophical bachelor essay while preserving 30 EC of free choice. UCR studies several philosophical questions with cognition, politics and society, but has fewer specialist philosophy courses and no required philosophy thesis.

audience.programmeDescription: Study fundamental questions about knowledge, reality, morality and human life through Western philosophical traditions, critical reading, argument and independent philosophical research. This comparison uses the regular Dutch Filosofie curriculum.
audience.comparisonExplanation: Both UCR programmes include 45 EC of direct philosophy: Western philosophy, ethics, mind, emotion, free will and political philosophy. One adds cognition and interpretive reading; the other adds rights, institutions and public life. These are substantive but narrower philosophical routes. Empirical science, literature and legal or social studies complement philosophical inquiry; they do not replace Radboud’s extended philosophical-text sequence, dedicated epistemology and philosophy of science, specialist seminars or required philosophy thesis.

curriculum.limitation: Current annual curriculum; later offerings may change. Restricted choices shown are one permitted selection. RADAr and induction are additional 0-EC requirements. The ordinary first-year study-advice threshold is 44 EC; workgroups and practicals require 80% attendance. An optional internship can use up to 15 EC of open space, subject to nominal progression, a suitable student-found placement and programme approval.
